headline: Brought CIDER's ads in-house and tripled results
context: For CIDER, a fashion e-commerce brand, I rebuilt paid ads in-house after an agency's results fell 70%.

detail.overview: CIDER's paid ads on Naver and Kakao were run by an agency, but results had dropped about 70%. I took the whole channel in-house and rebuilt it end to end.
detail.problem: Agency-run paid ads had fallen about 70%, with no reliable in-house tracking.
actions: Rebuilt Naver and Kakao paid campaigns in-house from scratch
Rebuilt conversion tracking to trust the numbers again
Ran A/B tests to improve ad performance steadily
impact: Grew ad performance 200% year over year
Kept improving about 26% month over month on average

headline: Rebuilt influencer playbook, sales jumped 67%
context: For CIDER, a fashion brand, I built the influencer marketing playbook and tracking from scratch.

detail.overview: CIDER's influencer marketing on Naver (a popular Korean blog platform) had no playbook or reliable tracking. I built sponsorship rules, a tier chart, and ways to measure results.
detail.problem: Naver results were hard to track directly, and each influencer campaign started from zero with no repeatable process.
actions: Wrote sponsorship guidelines so content stayed varied and on-brand
Built an influencer tier chart with clear performance metrics
Tracked results by hand since Naver couldn't measure them directly
impact: Sales rose 67% versus the previous campaign
Playbook adopted across Naver, Instagram, and YouTube

headline: Built an ambassador program that made 9x sales
context: For CIDER, a fashion brand, I ran an ambassador program from planning to launch as project lead.

detail.overview: CIDER had little brand awareness or loyalty in Korea. I ran an ambassador program end to end to build engagement, an exclusive collection, and steady ad content.
detail.problem: The brand needed deeper engagement, a reason to explore the app, and a steady flow of ad content.
actions: Designed the program around engagement, an exclusive collection, and content
Prepared over 20 styled looks with team feedback
Set reward tiers and routed content to ad teams
impact: Sales reached 9x the invested budget
Content mix beat targets at 52% feed, 47% reels

headline: Ran a pop-up that tripled competitors' foot traffic
context: For CIDER, a fashion brand, I led a Seoul pop-up event on a lean budget.

detail.overview: CIDER needed a big splash before pop-ups at two festivals, on a tight budget. Offline pop-up results (like foot traffic) are hard to measure, so I built a way to track it.
detail.problem: The event had to make a big impression on a tight budget, and offline results are hard to measure.
actions: Pitched press coverage instead of paying for placement
Researched other pop-ups for format and merchandising ideas
Built a tracking framework and aligned KPIs across teams
impact: Social search volume jumped +7,243%
Foot traffic hit about 3x competitors' average

headline: Grew CIDER's Korean blog traffic by 81%
context: For CIDER, a fashion brand new to Korea, I grew its blog and handled early customer questions.

detail.overview: CIDER had no recognition in Korea and no customer support yet. I built Instagram-style blog content and answered customer questions myself until formal support existed.
detail.problem: Limited manpower and rising customer questions arrived at once, and the blog had to feel like the brand itself.
actions: Built relationships by commenting directly on influencer blogs
Made Instagram-style posts: trends, styling guides, travel picks
Answered exchanges, sizing, and FAQs as early customer service
impact: Daily blog visitors rose 81%
Follower count doubled within six months

headline: Lifted address form completion by 20%
context: For CIDER's Korean app, I fixed sizing, address entry, and the returns process for local shoppers.

detail.overview: CIDER's Korean app lacked local touches for sizing, address entry, and returns. I designed an automatic address tool, resized options for Korean shoppers, and mapped the full return journey.
detail.problem: Foreign-sized options and manual address entry created friction, and any change needed leadership approval.
actions: Specced an automatic address tool with the backend team
Tested checkout with and without the address tool
Mapped the full return journey against competitors, stage by stage
impact: Address tool lifted checkout completion by 20%
Leadership approved the fixes and moved forward

headline: Moved customer messages to Kakao, retention rose
context: For CIDER's Korean shoppers, I built messaging and support on KakaoTalk, Korea's top chat app.

detail.overview: CIDER only reached customers by email and app alerts, while Korean shoppers live on KakaoTalk (a popular chat app). I added Kakao messages, a support chatbot, and local-language customer service.
detail.problem: There was no Korean-language customer channel or support, even though local shoppers rely heavily on chat.
actions: Sent Kakao messages for payment, shipping, and reviews
Built a Kakao chatbot for common customer questions
Mapped over 10 competitors' messaging approaches
impact: Retention and payment success improved after launch
Chatbot cut direct inquiries and collected complaint data

headline: Turned customer interviews into an action plan
context: For CIDER, I ran customer interviews from planning to a final action plan.

detail.overview: CIDER needed real customer feedback (voice of the customer) to guide its product and marketing. I planned and ran the interviews myself, start to finish.
detail.problem: There was no structured way to gather deep feedback on the app and products from Korean customers.
actions: Planned and ran the interviews from start to finish
Collected detailed feedback on the app and products
Turned findings into a prioritized action plan
impact: Customer feedback became a concrete plan for the team

headline: Mapped a company's market share in a dashboard
context: Portfolio project: I cleaned sample sales data and built a market-share dashboard for a global brand.

detail.overview: This portfolio project analyzed a sample electronics brand against competitors using a benchmarking dataset. I cleaned five separate tables and built a dashboard to compare market share and growth.
detail.problem: Five separate data tables needed cleaning and linking before any insight was possible.
actions: Cleaned and reshaped raw data across five tables
Linked the tables and built a calendar table
Wrote formulas for growth, prior-year sales, and market share
impact: Mapped the brand at 48.55% share with 10.94% growth
Found Canada underpenetrated versus the US market

headline: Found why 26.86% of customers left
context: Portfolio project: I analyzed a US phone company's customer data to find why people were leaving.

detail.overview: This portfolio project studied why customers left a sample US phone company. I broke the losses down by age, plan, and location to find who was leaving and why.
detail.problem: Losses were rising in a competitive market, but no one had broken down who was leaving or why.
actions: Cleaned the data with a structured checklist
Grouped customers by age, plan, and location
Cross-checked losses against contract length and international activity
impact: Overall customer loss measured at 26.86%
Pinpointed high-risk groups: seniors and heavy data users

headline: Built an interactive sales dashboard in Excel
context: Portfolio project: I built an interactive sales dashboard with buttons and filters in Excel.

detail.overview: This portfolio project turned a large sales spreadsheet into an interactive dashboard for non-technical viewers. I added filters, charts, and clickable buttons instead of static charts.
detail.problem: Thousands of rows of sales data needed to be explorable by non-technical viewers, not just fixed charts.
actions: Built charts: waterfall, stacked bar, line, and map
Added filters and live text callouts for details
Coded clickable buttons and a color-theme switcher
impact: Delivered a full dashboard covering revenue and returns
Showed 67% on-time delivery and a 10% return rate

headline: Split customers into 5 useful groups
context: Portfolio project: I grouped customers into behavior-based segments using clustering methods in Python.

detail.overview: This portfolio project built a customer-segmentation model on a public marketing dataset so campaigns could be targeted by behavior. I compared several clustering methods and picked the one that split people most usefully.
detail.problem: A mixed customer base overlapped heavily, so raw charts gave no clean groups to act on.
actions: Engineered features like age, spending, and engagement
Compared several clustering methods side by side
Mapped each group to a marketing action
impact: Produced 5 clear, action-ready customer groups
Confirmed higher income links to higher spending

headline: Analyzed 39 job ads to rank top skills
context: Self-directed project: I collected 39 Tokyo job postings and ranked the skills employers wanted most.

detail.overview: This self-directed project looked at what international employers in Tokyo actually expect from data and business analysts. I collected 39 job postings and counted which skills came up most.
detail.problem: Skill expectations were anecdotal, with no data-backed view of what to prioritize learning.
actions: Collected 39 postings from international companies
Counted required skills and tools in a spreadsheet
Ranked programming languages and visualization tools by frequency
impact: SQL was required most often, ahead of Python
Confirmed bilingual ability as a baseline expectation

headline: Pinpointed day 60 as when repeat buying stops
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I analyzed purchase data to find when one-time buyers stop repurchasing.

detail.overview: The brand wanted to re-target customers who bought once and stopped. I studied purchase data to find the exact day repeat buying drops off, then sized and designed an ad audience around it.
detail.problem: The starting numbers were wrong (budget rules, timezones, product sizes), and an early check against an existing ad list was invalid.
actions: Fixed early data errors in rules, timezones, and product sizes
Found day 60 using a drop-off pattern, not guesswork
Designed an ad audience and a fair before/after test
impact: Designed the ad audience and test plan, not yet launched
Reframed the value as reusing budget, not new customers

headline: Turned 4,700 overlapping audiences into a clear plan
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I ranked ad audiences and designed which to add or drop.

detail.overview: An AI-run ad line picks its own audiences, and I had to find which ones actually work well. I ranked thousands of audiences fairly and designed a safe plan to expand or exclude them.
detail.problem: Simple counting broke down because each shopper belonged to over a hundred audiences at once, and audience names didn't match their real IDs.
actions: Replaced a confusing score with one plain, readable number.
Matched audiences by their real ID, not just their name.
Set a size limit so huge audiences couldn't skew the ranking.
impact: Delivered a clear expand-or-exclude plan balancing reach against results.
Live results after the changes went live were still pending.

headline: Proved a new-customer ad change worked, cost halved
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I measured whether a new-customer ad strategy worked despite a budget cut.
metrics: New customers per dollar nearly doubled
Cost per new customer fell half

detail.overview: The brand had stopped showing ads to past buyers to win new customers, and wanted proof it worked. I compared results before and after, using a similar campaign as a control group.
detail.problem: Sales fell so much overall that every simple number looked like a failure, even though the strategy might have been working underneath.
actions: Compared matching time periods before and after, avoiding sale-season noise.
Measured new-customer share instead of raw totals, since spending dropped.
Showed loyal customers stayed steady, ruling out a market crash.
impact: Delivered proof the new-customer strategy worked, even after the budget cut.
The main ad channel flipped from pricier to cheaper than the rest.

headline: Proved a system to stop repeat ads actually worked
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I checked whether an ad system stopped repeat views and fixed gaps.

detail.overview: A system shows each ad group only to people the earlier groups missed, like a waterfall. I checked whether it worked, then found new audiences it should include.
detail.problem: The first check used the wrong measurement and looked like a failure, and one audience meant to narrow reach was secretly reaching everyone.
actions: Re-measured using cross-group overlap instead of single-group repeat views.
Found and sized new audiences, then ranked them by size.
Proved one audience was broken, reaching everyone instead of a narrow group.
impact: Confirmed the system worked and should stay running.
Designed 22 new audiences and 8 new ad groups to add.

headline: Caught a fake advertising result before delivery
context: For a coffee brand in Japan, I analyzed video ad data and fixed a wrong result before it shipped.

detail.overview: The client's video ads sat on top of its regular display and search ads. I built a pipeline to check how many extra people the video ads reached, and whether they boosted sales.
detail.problem: Broken campaign IDs, wrong product tags, and a hidden ad placement made the numbers unreliable, and an early sales-lift claim turned out to be miscalculated.
actions: Fixed broken campaign data by matching names instead of broken IDs
Checked products by hand online instead of trusting price rules
Recomputed the sales-lift number and corrected it before delivery
impact: Delivered a defensible report the client team used with confidence
Stopped a false result from ever reaching the client

headline: Found 11 errors in Amazon's own official template
context: For a coffee brand in Japan, I checked Amazon's official ad-data query for errors before running it.

detail.overview: I once found a coding bug that gave wrong totals in an ad-data query. I used that lesson to check Amazon's own official version of a similar query before trusting it with real data.
detail.problem: Amazon's official query repeated the same bug pattern and also overstated results by mixing timing rules incorrectly.
actions: Wrote a checklist from a past bug's root cause.
Checked Amazon's official query line by line against it.
Rewrote the query, fixing all 11 errors found.
impact: Built a reusable checklist now used on every project.
Designed fixes were pending a final test run.

headline: Rebuilt online ad targeting so top customers get priority
context: For a pet nutrition brand in Japan, I redesigned how their online ads target customers before a big sale.

detail.overview: Ahead of a major sale, I reorganized which customers a pet brand's ads reach first. I measured overlap between new and existing customer lists, then fixed rule order so top-value customers get budget first.
detail.problem: New customer lists mostly overlapped with existing ones, and the targeting order didn't match how big each customer group really was.
actions: Measured how much new customer lists overlapped with existing ones
Reordered targeting rules so top customers get budget priority
Fixed two rules that were ranked in the wrong order
impact: Delivered the full targeting redesign for the team to launch
Wrote simple rules the team can reuse for future targeting

headline: Targeted new buyers ahead of a big sale
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I designed and built this shopper-targeting audience for Amazon ads.

detail.overview: Shoppers were browsing pages but not buying before a big sale. I built an ad audience of recent browsers with no purchase history to target as likely new customers.
detail.problem: A too-strict 'no purchase' rule could sweep in loyal customers just waiting to reorder, and the new audience showed almost no traffic at launch.
actions: Defined 'new customer' using the platform's own 365-day rule.
Fixed a broken query column after a console error.
Traced zero delivery step by step instead of rebuilding blindly.
impact: Audience went live before the sale; delivery results were still pending.
Designed a reusable way to read ad results around any big sale.

headline: Showed sales grew, not fell, and found why
context: For a pet nutrition brand in Japan, I investigated a reported drop in new-customer sales.

detail.overview: The client believed new-customer sales were falling and wanted to know why. I found total sales had actually grown, then traced the real story to a shift between ad channels and overlapping ad targeting.
detail.problem: The starting belief that new-customer sales were dropping was wrong, and it hid a shift between two ad channels.
actions: Broke total sales into quantity sold and price paid
Traced the change to one ad channel losing share
Measured how often the same customers saw competing ads
impact: Nine-slide report accepted by the manager and client
Pointed the fix toward ad targeting, not budget caps

headline: Proved showing ads again to viewers doubled views
context: For a pet food brand's ad team in Japan, I measured whether repeat-viewer ads truly worked.
metrics: Views per person more than doubled

detail.overview: A campaign re-showed ads to people who'd seen the brand online before. The client doubted it helped, so I tested whether it truly reached the right people and added extra views.
detail.problem: My first read said reach doubled but repeat views stayed flat, which didn't match how the campaign was built to work.
actions: Questioned a 'no change' result that didn't make sense.
Found new, lightly-viewed people were dragging down the average.
Locked the comparison group before launch and re-measured fairly.
impact: Confirmed the campaign reached the right people and lifted views.
Reviewed the test's code and flagged fixes before reporting numbers.

headline: Built a sales forecast that shows its own guesswork
context: For a pet nutrition brand in Japan, I built a full-year sales forecast requested by my manager.

detail.overview: My manager wanted next year's sales estimated from this year's results, then adjusted for big holiday sales events. I built the estimate so the guessed part is one labeled number, not hidden in the formula.
detail.problem: The needed multiplier for holiday sales couldn't be measured because last year's matching data no longer existed.
actions: Sorted 200 products into 9 objective groups automatically
Checked three ways to measure the holiday effect first
Turned the unmeasurable guess into one adjustable number
impact: Delivered a reusable forecast workbook awaiting manager sign-off
Made the spend data's limits clear so no one misreads it

headline: Found two ad stages that need more budget
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I measured how well ads reached shoppers at each stage.

detail.overview: A pet food brand runs ads across four buying stages (awareness, consideration, purchase, loyalty) and wanted to know how deeply each stage reaches shoppers. Leadership needed one trustworthy chart set to judge funding per stage.
detail.problem: Early charts used mismatched math, so the year-end summary chart didn't match the month-by-month trend chart, confusing what the numbers meant.
actions: Defined one clear way to measure each stage's reach
Rebuilt the math so every chart added up correctly
Turned results into plain advice on where to spend more
impact: Delivered a reconciled chart set leaders could trust and reuse.
Flagged two under-funded stages and one over-saturated stage for budget talks.

headline: Found the best number of times to show ads
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I checked ad-frequency rules using real ad data.

detail.overview: A pet food brand wanted to know how often to repeat an ad before it stops helping, using Amazon's ad data room (AMC). Different goals (awareness, consideration, purchase, loyalty) needed different limits.
detail.problem: The obvious approach (picking the frequency with best results) always said 'show more,' because heavy viewers already liked the product most.
actions: Measured how many views it took to reach most people
Checked three signals together, not just one, before deciding
Found repeat views mostly went to already-loyal customers, not new ones
impact: Confirmed the awareness limit was correct; recommended cutting the loyalty limit sharply.
Suggested moving saved budget toward reaching new customers instead.

headline: Seeing both ad types multiplied new customers by 6.7x
context: For a pet food brand's awareness ads in Japan, I tested reach, frequency, and audience design.

detail.overview: A pet food brand ran six types of awareness ads and wanted to know if reach, frequency, and budget were right. I also tested whether pairing two ad types worked better than either alone.
detail.problem: Reach and frequency numbers were defined two different ways, and it looked like the discovery ads and retargeting ads worked separately.
actions: Defined reach clearly so every channel could be compared fairly
Tested how often to repeat ads using three signals at once
Grouped viewers by which ad combo they saw, then compared results
impact: Client increased spend on discovery ads and added a follow-up ad link.
Withdrew a frequency increase before it reached the client.

headline: Follow-up ads reach 78% of new shoppers
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I checked whether follow-up ads and targeting were working.

detail.overview: A pet food brand runs separate ads for cat and dog owners and re-shows ads to shoppers who already saw one (retargeting). The client worried the setup wasn't working.
detail.problem: A quick check made retargeting look broken (only 7-8%), and cat and dog audiences overlapped more than expected in early-stage ads.
actions: Fixed a technical bug that broke the original measurement
Recalculated the ad-follow-up rate the right way, over 3 months
Traced the overlap to a shared audience list, not a bug
impact: Showed 4 in 5 shoppers really were reached by earlier ads.
Recommended splitting the shared audience list to fix true overlap.

headline: Sorted every one of 170+ ad campaigns correctly
context: For a pet food brand's ad account in Japan, I built rules to label every ad campaign.

detail.overview: A pet food brand runs 170+ ad campaigns with three different naming styles. Every campaign needed to be sorted into clear categories (brand, species, funnel stage) with none left unlabeled.
detail.problem: An old shortcut in the sorting rule quietly mislabeled campaigns, and early checks had wrongly said everything passed.
actions: Rebuilt the naming rule to avoid accidental letter matches
Reordered rules so specific labels won over general ones
Built a checker that flags any campaign left unsorted
impact: Reached zero unlabeled campaigns after fixing the hidden bug.
Escalated only 7 truly unclear names for manual review.

headline: Rebuilt 10 ad audiences; 8 out of 10 worked
context: For a global PC brand's Japan ads, via their agency, I redesigned who gets retargeted with new-customer ads.
metrics: Excluded buyers from the past year

detail.overview: Two customer lists a PC brand used for retargeting had shrunk too small to use. I rebuilt them with a fixed one-year no-purchase rule so anyone who converted would count as a genuinely new customer.
detail.problem: The old lists stopped delivering, and 'never bought' was only checked inside whatever short time window each list used.
actions: Answered the client using only documented facts, not guesses
Split the shopping window from the fixed one-year exclusion
Hand-checked every date boundary before sending the final lists
impact: Delivered 8 of 10 working audience lists with documented logic
Built the exclusion rule to match the client's own definition

headline: Showed that showing ads more often reached fewer people
context: For a whisky brand's ad team in Japan, I tested what happened when we stopped limiting repeat ads.
metrics: Repeat views per person nearly doubled

detail.overview: A whisky brand had been limiting how many times each person saw its awareness ads, then removed that limit to see if performance improved. I compared two matched two-week periods, before and after, to check.
detail.problem: There was no side-by-side comparison group since the limit was removed for everyone at once, risking a misleading before/after read.
actions: Compared two equal 14-day windows, right before and after.
Picked cost-per-person-reached as the fairest scorecard for budgets.
Double-checked odd zero-result queries before trusting any numbers.
impact: Found the cheaper ads were repeating on the same people.
Recommended bringing the viewing limit back.

headline: Rescued a hidden low-budget channel from disappearing in reports
context: For a pet nutrition brand in Japan, I fixed data bugs and built a fairer way to score ad channels.
metrics: One path was half of it

detail.overview: A standard top-20 report by traffic volume made a cheap, effective ad channel invisible. I built a separate scorecard so small-budget channels could still be judged fairly, after also fixing two silent data bugs.
detail.problem: Ranking channels by traffic volume alone hid a small, cheap channel that mattered, and two hidden bugs were producing impossible numbers.
actions: Found why 'buyers' count matched pure traffic count exactly
Traced a data-naming bug that made purchases show as zero
Built a separate scorecard so small channels stayed visible
impact: Delivered a report structure that didn't hide the small channel
Fixed two bugs that were producing impossible numbers

headline: Fixed a data mix-up that hid video ad sales
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I built and debugged a dashboard matching two ad data systems.

detail.overview: I built a query that pulls all ad spending and sales into the same categories the client's dashboard uses. Then I compared every number side by side to catch mismatches.
detail.problem: Video ad results were silently mislabeled as a different category, and even after fixing that, sales still didn't fully match.
actions: Combined spending and sales data into one matching table
Traced why video sales showed as zero, found mislabeling
Compared rankings before and after to confirm decisions stayed sound
impact: Query adopted as the team's standard dashboard, category counts now match perfectly
Remaining sales gap accepted since rankings didn't change

headline: Proved a streaming ad's 'exclusive reach' claim was inflated
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I tested whether one ad format truly reached new people.
metrics: About half of two groups overlapped

detail.overview: A streaming-ad format claimed to reach people no other ad touched. I re-ran the numbers without a channel that was quietly inflating the overlap, and checked whether each funnel step really fed the next.
detail.problem: An early estimate said a video ad format was mostly unique reach, but that number actually measured overlap, not exclusivity.
actions: Removed a channel that was distorting the overlap numbers
Recalculated true exclusive reach versus shared reach for each format
Checked how much each funnel step fed into the next
impact: Corrected the reach claim and confirmed the retargeting funnel works as intended

headline: Fixed a report that shortchanged nighttime ad sales
context: For a pet nutrition brand in Japan, I rebuilt an ad report so night-time sales counted correctly.

detail.overview: A report judged ad success by purchase time, making quiet night hours look worse than they were. I rebased it on exposure time instead, after tracing three reasons it first returned no data.
detail.problem: Measuring success by purchase time under-credited quiet hours, and the new query first returned nothing for three separate reasons.
actions: Tracked down three separate causes of the empty report
Fixed a purchase filter that missed most real sales
Removed an average number that a privacy rule was hiding
impact: Validated the hourly report against the ad platform's own numbers
Designed a spend-linked version that has not been run yet

headline: Cut unsorted ad campaigns from 13 down to zero
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I built the monthly ad-report data pipeline and campaign-sorting rules.

detail.overview: A monthly ad report needed cost and sales split by brand, pet type, and funnel stage. I wrote sorting rules in Amazon's ad data room (AMC) and checked results until none were left unsorted.
detail.problem: Campaign names weren't standardized, so a simple rule missed many campaigns, and cost and sales data lived in separate systems.
actions: Wrote rules to sort campaigns by brand, pet type, and stage.
Tested results repeatedly and fixed rules until nothing was unsorted.
Matched cost data to sales data using the same grouping rules.
impact: Delivered a fully sorted campaign report with cost and sales combined.
Standardized how key report numbers were defined across the report.

headline: Built a 2,700-product competitor list and picked targets
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I built and classified a competitor product list for ad targeting.

detail.overview: I gathered thousands of competitor products from Amazon Japan and sorted them into the client's product categories automatically. Then I picked 40 products, mixing popular and niche ones, for ad targeting.
detail.problem: Automatically sorting messy product names into the right category was hard, especially when the client's own labels did not match my rules.
actions: Designed search terms to find competitor products, not our own
Built a sorting system that classified products by product name
Merged two product lists and picked 40 for targeting
impact: Delivered a clean competitor list and a ready targeting shortlist
Found the client's category definitions did not match ours

headline: Showed which product line turns budget into sales best
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I analyzed whether ad budget changes tracked with new-customer sales results.

detail.overview: A client asked if ad budget changes matched new-to-brand (first-time buyer) sales changes, by product line and channel. I reframed it as three questions: where money goes, where sales come from, and how they connect.
detail.problem: Only three months of data existed, budget mattered across five different levels, and the two ad channels used different naming.
actions: Rebuilt clean monthly totals by removing duplicate subtotal rows.
Compared each segment's spend share against its sales share.
Rewrote conclusions to avoid overstating cause from only 3 months.
impact: Delivered a clear view of which segments turn budget into sales best.
Kept conclusions honest by not claiming strong correlation from 3 data points.

headline: Fixed a data illusion that hid true buying speed
context: For a premium coffee brand in Japan, I measured how fast people buy after seeing an ad.

detail.overview: A client asked how long after seeing an ad people take to buy. My first pass looked wrong because it ignored the 14-day tracking window and counted recent, still-unfinished cases.
detail.problem: Sales counted past the 14-day tracking window aren't valid, and very recent ad views hadn't had time to finish tracking yet.
actions: Cut out sales that fell outside the 14-day window.
Excluded recent ad views whose tracking wasn't finished yet.
Simplified time groups from 37 down to 11 categories.
impact: Delivered a trustworthy buying-speed model; final chart is not yet finished.

headline: Video ads were cheaper to show, but converted less
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I compared video and static ads to guide budget.
metrics: Video reach cost: half of Static

detail.overview: I traced each customer's ad journey (path to purchase) to see whether video or static ads worked better. I split the data by ad type instead of just campaign, then compared costs and results.
detail.problem: The usual report only showed ad campaigns, not video vs static, so nobody could tell which creative type actually worked.
actions: Rebuilt the ad-tracking query to label each ad as video or static
Fixed a cost formula so it reflected real billed spending
Wrote plain-language slides and a script explaining the tradeoffs
impact: Recommended keeping video ads steady, boosting them only during sales periods
Set a reusable rule for measuring any ad type by customer journey

headline: Ranked ad channels to build three budget plans
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I scored ad channels to propose three 2026 budget plans.

detail.overview: The client wanted to know which ad channels to grow and which to protect for the next year's budget. I scored each channel on cost and new-customer results, then built three budget plans.
detail.problem: Six months of data made comparing channels unfair, since view counts and spend naturally differ by channel size.
actions: Adjusted for time so channels could be fairly compared
Built a simple scoring system based on cost and reach
Drafted three budget plans balancing sales and new customers
impact: Delivered three ready-to-review budget plans with clear scoring logic
Designed shared rules other channel-scoring projects later reused

headline: Grouped 174 products to guide next year's budget
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I grouped products to show where ad budget should go.

detail.overview: A brand had 174 products and needed to know which ones actually bring in new customers. I grouped them into three simple types and built a one-page chart to guide 2026 ad spending.
detail.problem: Ranking products by new-customer rate alone put tiny, barely-selling items at the top, which was misleading.
actions: Filtered out tiny products before ranking by new-customer rate.
Sorted the rest into three plain, easy-to-understand groups.
Built one chart and rewrote rules for a second product line.
impact: Gave the client a clear one-page plan for 2026 ad budget.
Repeated the grouping for a second product line with new rules.

headline: Rebuilt a sale budget to avoid wasted spend
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I checked and redesigned a client's holiday sale spending plan.
metrics: Weak week's budget capped, not grown

detail.overview: A client's first-ever sale budget plan fell short of its own sales target. I checked the numbers against real past data and redesigned how the budget was split by day and product line.
detail.problem: There was no past sale to compare against, and cramming the same total budget into fewer days changes its effect.
actions: Rejected the client's overly pessimistic sales assumptions using real data.
Compared daily spending, not totals, to judge the real risk.
Capped the weak week's budget and moved money to the strong one.
impact: Designed a daily budget plan that better protects sales results.
Gave the client a data-backed answer instead of guesswork.

headline: Explained why 'new customer' ads seemed to fail
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I investigated a confusing result in a customer-acquisition ad campaign.

detail.overview: Ads meant to reach brand-new shoppers were set to exclude anyone who bought recently, yet most buyers still looked like repeat customers. I dug into why the numbers didn't match the setup.
detail.problem: The report showed mostly repeat buyers even though the targeting excluded them, and the cause could be our setup or a defined difference.
actions: Separated two different percentages that were being confused together.
Ruled out simple explanations using logic, not guesswork.
Asked Amazon one yes-or-no question to pinpoint the cause.
impact: Designed a question so any Amazon answer points to a clear next step.
Gave managers a simple, two-number explanation for the year-end review.

headline: Tested whether one ad type was stealing credit
context: For a global PC brand in Japan, I checked whether a premium ad campaign was gaming attribution credit.

detail.overview: A media partner suspected one premium ad type just grabbed credit for sales other ads had already earned. I rebuilt the tracking query and designed a before/after test to check.
detail.problem: An AI query-writing tool kept breaking the customer-journey logic, mixing up campaign groups and losing the correct time order.
actions: Split the work: one AI writes rules, another builds queries.
Listed every campaign name explicitly instead of guessing patterns.
Designed a before/after comparison to test the partner's suspicion.
impact: Delivered a corrected query, though final results are still pending.
Designed a fair test to prove credit-stealing versus real extra sales.

headline: Found which months ads helped, not hurt, sales
context: For a pet food brand in Japan, I was the analyst answering whether ads were stealing sales.

detail.overview: Checked whether more Amazon ad spend was quietly stealing sales that would have happened anyway (organic sales), for a pet food brand's Japan team. Built a simple monthly score instead of one big average.
detail.problem: The client was sure rising ad spend was cannibalizing organic sales, but looking at all months together hid the real monthly pattern.
actions: Pulled 13 months of ad and organic sales data.
Rejected a 'no effect' claim that ignored bad months.
Built a monthly score comparing total sales change to ad spend change.
impact: Turned 'ads hurt sales' into a month-by-month spending plan.
Found one product line was more prone to losing organic sales.

headline: Found the simplest chart clients could actually use
context: For the same brand, I tested spend-response curves, then switched to a simpler monthly scorecard.

detail.overview: I fit several math curves to find the point where more ad spending stops paying off. With limited data points, the curves kept changing shape, so I used a simpler chart instead.
detail.problem: With only 13 months of data, the fitted curve kept changing its answer whenever the target efficiency level changed.
actions: Fit several curve shapes to the monthly spend and sales data.
Removed one early month as a data-collection outlier.
Replaced the unstable curve with a clearer monthly chart.
impact: Set the groundwork for a seasonal budget shift plan.
Curve numbers stayed unverified, so a simpler chart was used instead.

headline: Built an Excel tool clients could test themselves
context: For the same brand, I built a self-serve Excel tool so the client could test budget changes.

detail.overview: I turned a complex sales-response chart into a simple Excel tool: the client types in a budget change and instantly sees expected sales and a color-coded verdict. It took several redesigns to get it right.
detail.problem: Early versions broke basic logic: they showed the same result every month, or profitable results for the wrong month.
actions: Required the tool to match real sales at zero change.
Used each month's real baseline instead of a made-up average.
Removed profit-margin guesses, judging results by sales impact only.
impact: Gave the client a self-serve tool for monthly budget calls.
Forecasts are model-based, not yet tested against real spending.

headline: Found why ad sales numbers didn't match the report
context: For the same pet food brand, I fixed why our ad data didn't match the client's report.

detail.overview: Our ad platform's data room (AMC) showed 43% more ad sales than the client's official monthly report for the same month. I traced it to purchases being counted twice.
detail.problem: One purchase was sometimes counted under two different ad types, inflating the ad sales number well above the client's report.
actions: Split ad sales by ad type to find the overlap.
Set a rule so each purchase counts only once.
Rebuilt the data pull as two separate, checkable steps.
impact: Traced the gap to double-counted purchases across ad channels.
Created a reusable checklist for building future queries safely.
